title: Xi Jinping calls for global AI cooperation, slams U.S. tech curbs as ‘overstretching’ security
summary:
Chinese President Xi Jinping used his keynote at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on Friday to pitch China as a champion of inclusive AI development, while sharply criticizing U.S. restrictions on technology sharing. “The development of artificial intelligence should not be a solo performance by any single country but rather a symphony of global cooperation,” Xi said, repeating Beijing’s longstanding complaint that Washington is “overstretching the concept of national security” to hobble China’s tech rise.

The speech came as U.S.-led export controls have cut off China from advanced semiconductors and AI tools, intensifying the rivalry between the world’s two largest economies. In response, Xi announced concrete steps: China will provide 30 countries access to a Chinese-developed AI meteorological early warning system and offer 5,000 AI training opportunities to developing nations over five years. He also unveiled the new World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, an intergovernmental body headquartered in Shanghai and signed by 29 countries including Pakistan, Russia, and Kazakhstan.

Analysts see the organization as a direct counter to the U.S.-led Pax Silica framework, which includes Japan, the U.K., Australia, and others. “China will not let America be the monopoly of AI technology,” said George Chen of The Asia Group. The conference, running through Monday, showcases China’s growing self-reliance: Huawei displayed its Atlas 950 SuperPoD AI computing system, and startup Moonshot released Kimi K3, claiming it is the world’s largest open-source model with 2.8 trillion parameters — surpassing DeepSeek’s V4 Pro. Such moves challenge U.S. dominance, though American officials accuse Chinese firms of illicit “distillation” of U.S. models, a charge Beijing denies.

Xi’s outreach to the Global South underscores a strategic push to shape global AI governance on China’s terms, even as both nations recently agreed to a bilateral AI dialogue following Trump’s May visit to Beijing.
why_it_matters: The global race for AI isn't just about technology—it shapes who sets the rules for the future internet, how jobs are created, and even how countries monitor citizens; as a teen, you'll live in a world where these power struggles affect what apps you can use, how your data is handled, and what career opportunities exist.

background_read: Xi Jinping has been the president of China since 2013, and he has pushed for China to become a world leader in technology, especially artificial intelligence.
The World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai is a major annual event where Chinese tech companies and officials showcase their latest AI breakthroughs.

Since 2019, the U.S. has used export controls to block Chinese companies like Huawei from getting advanced American chips and AI software, saying China might use them for military purposes or surveillance.
The 'Pax Silica' framework is a recent U.S.-led effort that brings together allies like Japan, the U.K., and Australia to set rules for AI development—rules that often exclude China.
The term 'Global South' refers to developing countries, many in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, that China is courting as partners in its tech and diplomatic expansion.

perspectives.description: China argues that sharing AI tools like weather warning systems helps developing countries save lives and grow their economies. By offering training and open-source models, Beijing claims to make AI a global public good rather than a weapon controlled by a few rich nations.

The United States and its allies worry that China will use AI cooperation to spread its surveillance technology and military advantages. They allege Chinese firms steal American breakthroughs through 'distillation' and that China's AI governance model could undermine democratic values and privacy worldwide.

The rivalry reveals how AI has become a new sphere of great-power competition, similar to the nuclear arms race of the Cold War. Historically, when two superpowers build rival technological blocs, the world splits into parallel systems, which can slow global cooperation on safety standards and risk management.

As more countries join either the Chinese or U.S.-led AI group, we may see a digital iron curtain where AI systems cannot work together. If diplomatic talks succeed, both sides might agree on shared safety rules, but if not, the world could see a messy patchwork of incompatible AI regulations that stifles innovation.
